claims.text: A periodic array of coherent or semi-coherent multilayer interfaces pins dislocations in HEA coatings.
Multilayer interfaces slow diffusion-mediated processes in HEA coatings.
Interfacial dislocation pinning and suppression of diffusion cause resistance to creep.
The relevant multilayer can consist of layers having essentially identical alloy composition while retaining well-defined interfaces.
A homogeneous coating with equivalent composition and thickness is an appropriate control for isolating the effect of the multilayer interfaces.
The interfaces act as physical barriers to the migration and collective motion of dislocations.
Multilayer interfaces may disrupt diffusion pathways relative to a homogeneous HEA.
Dislocations generated during loading are blocked or redirected at multilayer interfaces.
Blocking or redirecting dislocations at interfaces limits the propagation of slip avalanches.
Homogeneous HEAs can deform through jerky slip avalanches within a specific range of temperature and strain rate.
HEAs possess intrinsic sluggish diffusion that further suppresses time-dependent deformation.
The multilayer coating will have a lower creep strain rate than a homogeneous HEA coating under identical conditions.
The multilayer coating will show a delayed onset of plastic flow under constant load relative to the homogeneous coating.
Dislocation pile-ups will form at the multilayer interfaces.
Homogeneous HEA coatings lacking periodic internal interfaces have higher creep rates.
The proposed mechanism applies while interfaces remain stable and dislocation-mediated plasticity dominates.
Very high temperatures or prolonged exposure may degrade the interfaces and diminish their creep-resistance effect.
The effectiveness of interfacial strengthening depends on interfacial structure and layer thickness.
